strip: 3-D handpump trains, one 8-core case at a time (~28 min each)
goal: A Venturi, changed in bore shape only, for the handpump that never overflows and doses very consistently, and that also doses consistently on steady piped flow from 6 to 100 L/min. Method: Stage 1 Venturi alone (2-D), Stage 2 the steady pipe rig (3-D), Stage 3 the handpump hardware (3-D + pulse model). No fixed date: the winners are bench tested when ready and the lab data feeds the next iteration.

rows: ≤ 2.67× (aim ~1.6×, the best a fixed shape can do)
None within the pump range (to ~26 L/min)
requirements.note: Spread = highest ÷ lowest dose on piped flow, with the feed law measured on the bench (chlorine flow ∝ suction^0.73). Current part measured to 100 L/min in 2-D (no extrapolation); candidates in 2-D and 3-D. Status is for the new design: piped consistency must match or beat the current part, and the handpump must not overflow.

findings: Stage 2 complete: E and F (13 mm throats) tie at ~1.6× on the pipe rig.

Pipe rig (straight 1" pipe → 1" NPT elbow), 3-D, port side, 6–100 L/min: F 1.59×, E 1.60×, C 1.69×, A 1.71×, V1 1.75× (current part 1.86× in 2-D). E is limited by its 6 L/min end, F by its 100 L/min end. F is more sensitive to port clocking (17% inside/outside of the bend vs E 11%); F's 20 mm outlet keeps the outlet fuller at 6 L/min. Stage 3 (handpump) decides.
Stage 1 converged: 13–13.5 mm throat with a 20–22 mm outlet nozzle.

Round 3 tried every remaining bore freedom one at a time (diffuser 3/5/6°, 15° inlet cone, throat 8/22 mm, port 3.5 mm down): nothing beats its base by more than 1%. The best two both move the port slightly upstream. On the pipe rig the elbow tips the optimum to 13 mm (E, 1.60×).
Current part measured to 100 L/min: 1.86× spread, and its throat reaches vapour pressure at ~100 L/min.

2-D (straight pipe) runs of the current part to 120 L/min: dose spread 6–100 L/min = 1.86× (lowest at 20, highest at 100). The minimum wall pressure is −98.7 kPa gauge at 100 L/min (vapour limit) and impossible at 120, so the current part cannot really run at 100 L/min without cavitating. The new candidates stay at −60 to −78 kPa at 100 L/min in 2-D (13.5 mm −60 to −66, 13 mm −71 to −78) and spread 1.63–1.70×.
Round 1: 13.5–14 mm throats with a 20–23 mm outlet are all within 1.64–1.76×.

Best that keeps the outlet full at 6 L/min: 13.5 mm throat, 20 mm outlet, 1.64× over 6–100 L/min (the best a fixed bore can do is 1.62×). The optimum is broad, so print tolerances matter little. Wider (15–16 mm) and narrower (12.5 mm) throats are worse.
The feed law is now measured.
The current part's pipe-flow bench curves fit chlorine flow ∝ suction^0.73 (within 5%). Neither the viscous (n = 1) nor the orifice (n = 0.5) assumption fits.
Handpump: the dose doubles once the head fills, and overflow follows within ~2 L/min.

Upgraded pulse model (two-phase priming rule + measured feed law) reproduces the V1 handpump bench within ~25% (model/bench mg/L at the port side: 0.23/0.31, 0.94/0.93, 1.02/1.32). A design whose head never fills over the pump's flow range doses most evenly; V1 stays in that regime up to ~29 L/min.
The current part is consistent on piped flow; its problem is overflow.
Measured 1.3–1.5× from 6 to 38 L/min, and the CFD + feed law reproduces that. It overflows the Afridev at 18.5 L/min.
Best fixed shape: about a 13 mm throat.
With n = 0.73 the flattest Venturi spans 6–100 L/min at about 1.6×. In the 1" V-layout that's a throat of about 13–13.5 mm. Large throats (V2, V3) are worse, not better.
Handpump weak dosing is air, not suction.
When the pump-head level drops below the inlet bore, air reaches the Venturi and the dose halves (two-phase CFD).
